title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan Warns AI Hardware Shortage Will Last Two To Three Years
author: M
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has warned that shortages of AI hardware could persist for another two to three years, highlighting the strain that rapid infrastructure expansion is placing on the semiconductor supply chain. Speaking at a DBS conference in Singapore on October 12, Tan said constraints would continue as the industry struggles to meet demand for AI computing equipment.

His outlook points to a prolonged imbalance between demand and available production. Reporting on the remarks identified memory, wafers and advanced packaging as areas facing capacity constraints. These bottlenecks suggest that increasing chip output alone may be insufficient to resolve the shortage.

Tan also stressed that the sector must demonstrate a return on investment. Alongside Broadcom CEO Hock Tan, he raised concerns about financing conditions, including rising borrowing costs, even as near-term demand for AI infrastructure remains strong.

The implication is that the AI industry faces two connected tests: securing enough equipment to expand and generating enough economic value to justify that expansion. Heavy spending can create revenue for hardware suppliers while leaving buyers with substantial costs that take years to recover.

For businesses adopting AI, the relevant measures include productivity improvements, lower operating expenses and additional revenue. More computing capacity matters commercially when it helps deliver those outcomes. Purchasing hardware or deploying a model does not, by itself, establish that an investment has succeeded.

For investors, Tan’s comments suggest caution about treating shortages as proof of lasting profitability. Scarcity can support suppliers’ sales, but customers still need sustainable business models.

His warning therefore reinforces both the strength and the uncertainty of the AI boom. Demand appears capable of sustaining infrastructure investment for several years, while the longer-term outlook depends on whether AI applications deliver measurable financial benefits. The industry’s next challenge is converting today’s spending into durable economic returns.

Speaking at a DBS event in Singapore, Tan also predicted quantum computing could go mainstream within the next three to five years.
